summary: Unlike X.509 certificates, the Cryptographic Message Syntax is vulnerable to algorithm substitution attacks, in which an attacker changes the algorithm or its parameters to alter a signature check. This standards-track document defines a signed attribute that protects the algorithm identifiers, so tampering can be detected.

plainLanguage.summary: If a thief could swap the lock-checking method on your documents, a fake could pass. This adds a seal covering which method was used, so swaps are noticed.

questions: what is an algorithm substitution attack
how to protect cms signature algorithm

where must the cms algorithm protection attribute be placed
subtitle: A signed copy of the algorithm names, so an attacker cannot quietly swap in a weaker hash or signature algorithm.

tldr.problem: In the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) the algorithm identifiers are not always covered by the signature, so an attacker could swap the algorithm or its parameters and change the result of a signature check.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6211 defines a signed (or authenticated) attribute, CMSAlgorithmProtection, that holds a copy of the algorithm identifiers. A validator that supports it compares the copy with the real fields and fails if they differ.
tldr.outcome: The algorithm choices become protected by the signature or message authentication code. The RFC says that at the time there was no known method to exploit this kind of attack.

today: RFC 6211 is a Proposed Standard, published in April 2011, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Algorithm Substitution Problem
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), unlike X.509/PKIX certificates, is vulnerable to algorithm substitution attacks. In such an attack the attacker changes the algorithm being used, or its parameters, in order to change the result of a signature verification.

X.509 certificates avoid this because the signature algorithm is duplicated in the TBSCertificate.signature field, and the validator must compare both copies. RFC 6211 gives CMS a similar protection by defining an attribute that carries a copy of the relevant algorithm identifiers, so the signature or authentication process covers them.
sections.plainLanguage: Certificates already write down which method they used and double-check it. This RFC teaches another kind of message to do the same.

sections.title: How the Attack Works
sections.content:
The attacker looks for a different algorithm that produces the same result as the one the signer used. For example, if the signer hashed the content with SHA-1, the attacker looks for another hash algorithm with an output of the same length but with which collisions are easier to find. The RFC names SHA-0 and RIPEMD-160 as other algorithms with a hash value of the same length. Parameterized algorithm identifiers can be attacked in a similar way.

The RFC expects such attacks to be aimed at items that are both long term and high value, and more likely at older documents, since the algorithms used when the message was signed degrade over time. Countersigning does not help, because a countersignature signs only the signature value, while this attack leaves the signature value alone and changes the algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: A cheater tries to find a different, weaker way of checking that gives the same answer. Adding a second signature on top does not help, because the cheater never touched the signature itself.

sections.title: What SignerInfo Already Protects
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the fields of the CMS SignerInfo structure to see which are covered by the signature.

  • version is not protected, but many implementations ignore it.
  • sid can be protected with either version of the signing certificate attribute.
  • digestAlgorithm has been protected only implicitly, because CMS defined one digest algorithm per hash length and there is an unwritten convention to use the same digest algorithm for content and signature. If newer algorithms give several choices for one hash length, or add parameters, much of that implicit protection is lost.
  • signatureAlgorithm was protected by implication, for example RSA keys implied the RSA v1.5 signature. This is no longer true with the RSA-PSS signature algorithms.
  • signedAttrs are directly protected; unsignedAttrs are explicitly not.

So the digest and signature algorithm fields were protected only indirectly, and the new attribute makes that protection explicit. It also covers the macAlgorithm field of the AuthenticatedData structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Some parts of a message were already sealed, but the note saying which sealing method was used only worked by habit. This RFC writes that note down properly.

sections.title: The CMSAlgorithmProtection Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute has the ASN.1 type CMSAlgorithmProtection, a sequence with a required digestAlgorithm, an optional signatureAlgorithm (tag 1) and an optional macAlgorithm (tag 2). Exactly one of signatureAlgorithm or macAlgorithm SHALL be present. It is identified by an object identifier under the pkcs9 arc, ending in 52.

  • digestAlgorithm copies the digest algorithm field, including parameters.
  • signatureAlgorithm copies SignerInfo.signatureAlgorithm and is used only in SignerInfo.signedAttrs.
  • macAlgorithm copies AuthenticatedData.macAlgorithm and is used only in AuthenticatedData.authAttrs.

The attribute MUST have a single attribute value, and it MUST be a signed or authenticated attribute, never an unsigned, unauthenticated or unprotected one. Each SignedAttributes or AuthAttributes set MUST include only one instance of it.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute is a small card listing the checking method that was used. It has to sit inside the sealed part of the message, and there can only be one card.

sections.title: Verification Rules
sections.content:
A CMS validator that supports the attribute MUST do extra checks. For signed data, SignerInfo.digestAlgorithm and SignerInfo.signatureAlgorithm MUST each be compared with the matching field in the attribute, and if they are not the same (modulo encoding) signature validation MUST fail. For authenticated data, AuthenticatedData.digestAlgorithm and AuthenticatedData.macAlgorithm are compared in the same way, and authentication MUST fail on a mismatch.

Two rules apply to the comparison. A field with a default value MUST compare as identical whether it is defaulted or explicit, so a plain binary compare of the encoded bytes is not enough. And for algorithms such as SHA-1, where some implementations include a NULL parameter and others omit it, the RFC leaves it to the implementer to decide whether equality is satisfied, noting that the same implementation normally produces both encodings.
sections.plainLanguage: The checker reads the card and the message side by side. If they name different methods, or are even a little different in an unexpected way, the message is rejected.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The document addresses algorithm substitution by an attacker. The RFC says that at the time there was no known method to exploit this type of attack, but if one succeeded, a weaker algorithm could replace a stronger one, or parameters could be changed to alter the behavior of the hashing algorithm. One example given is changing the initial parameter value for the hash functions with parameters of RFC 6210.

The attribute only helps when it is placed where the signature or message authentication code protects it. In an unsigned or unauthenticated location it adds no security. For IANA, all identifiers are assigned out of the S/MIME OID arc.
sections.plainLanguage: The card only helps if it is locked inside the sealed part. If it is left outside, a cheater can change it too.

data.title: CMSAlgorithmProtection
data.code:
CMSAlgorithmProtection ::= SEQUENCE {
    digestAlgorithm         DigestAlgorithmIdentifier,
    signatureAlgorithm  [1] SignatureAlgorithmIdentifier OPTIONAL,
    macAlgorithm        [2] MessageAuthenticationCodeAlgorithm
                                     OPTIONAL
}
(WITH COMPONENTS { signatureAlgorithm PRESENT,
                   macAlgorithm ABSENT } |
 WITH COMPONENTS { signatureAlgorithm ABSENT,
                   macAlgorithm PRESENT })
